name: Converse–Wood-Smith otoplasty

lead: This otoplasty cuts through ear cartilage in parallel lines and uses tubing sutures so the cartilage forms an antihelical fold. It stems from Converse's 1955 work.
Only animal research and general descriptions were found.

paras: Full-thickness cartilage incisions let it bend into a fold held by sutures.
Surgeons report hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity concerns with cartilage-cutting methods, which contributed to a shift toward suture-only techniques.

studies.title: Histomorphology of neochondrogenesis after antihelical fold creation: a comparison of three otoplasty techniques in the rabbit.

lead: The Converse–Wood-Smith technique forms an antihelix by making full-thickness incisions through the ear cartilage and shaping it with tubing sutures. Wikipedia describes it as two parallel cartilage incisions with sutures that create a more natural fold; Converse described a cartilage-incision method in 1955.[1]

It belongs to the cartilage-cutting group of otoplasty methods. Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting techniques carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which led to growing use of suture-based methods.

paras: Wikipedia places the technique with cartilage-scoring methods, using two parallel incisions with tubing sutures to form the fold.[1]
A rabbit study compared three antihelical-fold otoplasty techniques and examined new cartilage growth and whether recurrence related to the method or the duration of suture fixation.[2]
No studies found. One animal study (rabbits) compared otoplasty techniques histologically.[2]
